Over Days 8 and 9 your team builds one notebook: it takes a dataset nobody in the room has seen,
walks it through the ten steps, and ends with a figure and a claim. On Friday afternoon each team
walks the class through theirs.

This page is the description of the finished thing. The [project
kickoff](interactive-sessions/7d_project_kickoff.qmd) covers choosing a team, a dataset and a
question. [Day 8](day8.qmd) and [Day 9](day9.qmd) carry the hour-by-hour plan.

## What you are building

One Jupyter notebook, per team, named `Project_<team name>.ipynb`.

It is **self-contained**: somebody who has your notebook and nothing else can restart the kernel,
run every cell from the top, and get your figures back. Self-containment matters more than
anything else on this page, and it is the property most often lost, usually to a cell that was
deleted after the variable it defined was already in memory.

It is **documented**: markdown cells explain what each step was for and what it found, and code
comments explain anything a reader could not work out from the code.

It uses **pandas, numpy, matplotlib and seaborn**, and nothing else. Avoid analyses that need
mapping.

## The ten steps

Every one of the ten steps appears in the notebook under its own markdown heading, in this order,
even where the honest content of a step is one sentence.

1. Import Data
2. Explore Data
3. Clean Data
4. Filter Data
5. Sort Data
6. Transform Data
7. Group Data
8. Aggregate Data
9. Join / Reshape Data
10. Visualize Data

These are the same ten steps described on [The Data Science
Workflow](the-data-science-workflow.qmd).

Step 9 is the one most likely to be short. If your project uses a single table and needs neither a
join nor a reshape, write that under the heading and move on. Step 3 is the next most likely: a
file that arrives clean has still been cleaned, and *"`.isnull().sum()` is zero in every column and
there are no duplicate rows"* is that step done properly. A step that is skipped silently is
different, because then nobody reading the notebook knows whether the work was unnecessary or
merely undone.

## What "done" looks like

This is a checklist, not a grading scheme. Nothing here is scored. It is the list I would use if
you asked me whether your notebook was finished, so you may as well have it.

**The notebook runs.**

- [ ] Restart the kernel, run all, no errors.
- [ ] Every dataset loads from a URL or a path that will still work on somebody else's machine.

**The ten steps are all there.**

- [ ] Ten markdown headings, in order, matching the list above.
- [ ] Under each, either the work or a sentence saying why the step needed none.

**The analysis answers a question you wrote down.**

- [ ] The question appears near the top, in a complete sentence, with your column names in it.
- [ ] The two questions you set aside are named, with a sentence on why.
- [ ] One sentence says what one row of the dataset represents.

**The figure carries the claim.**

- [ ] At least one figure made with seaborn or matplotlib.
- [ ] Axis labels with units where units exist.
- [ ] A title that states the finding rather than naming the variables.
- [ ] A legend, if you used `hue=`.

**The claim is stated and supported.**

- [ ] Two or three sentences near the top: what you asked, what you found, what it rests on.
- [ ] The counts behind any group comparison are visible somewhere in the notebook.
- [ ] The word *significant* does not appear, because you have not run a hypothesis test.

**Somebody else can read it.**

- [ ] No cells left over from an approach you abandoned.
- [ ] Markdown between the code, not just at the top.
- [ ] Every team member's name in the first cell.

## Handing it in

The notebook is due **before lunch on Friday, September 11**, when you push it. The whole morning
is available to finish in, and presentations are in the afternoon for that reason. There is nothing
to submit after class.

1. Put the project notebook in its **own repository**, separate from your coursework repository.
2. **Keep the outputs.** The [GitHub session](interactive-sessions/8a_github.qmd) has you
   configure `nbstripout`, which strips figures and printed output from every commit. Stripping
   output is right for coursework and wrong here, because your figures are the deliverable. Do not
   configure `nbstripout` on this repository.
3. Add a short `README.md`: the team, the dataset, its source URL, and the question.
4. Push, then open the repository in a browser. GitHub renders `.ipynb` directly, so you can
   confirm in ten seconds that the figures are showing.
5. Send me the repository URL.

## The presentation

**Twelve minutes, then three for questions.** Present from the notebook itself rather than from
slides, and see [Day 9](day9.qmd) for a walkthrough plan that fits the twelve minutes.

Additional figures are welcome, and you are encouraged to make the notebook engaging to read.
Exploratory figures belong under Step 2, where they were actually made.

## Finding a dataset

The five tests for a workable dataset are in the [project
kickoff](interactive-sessions/7d_project_kickoff.qmd), and they are worth applying before you
commit to anything: one CSV, more than a couple of hundred rows, at least two numeric columns, at
least one categorical column, and you can say what one row represents.

It does not need to be environmental data. Be curious.

### General collections

- [Kaggle datasets, filtered to CSV](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets?fileType=csv)
- [Data is Plural](https://www.data-is-plural.com/)
- [US Data.gov](https://data.gov/)
- [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/)
- [TidyTuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/master/data)

### Oddly specific, and all fine choices

- [Central Park Squirrel Census](https://www.thesquirrelcensus.com/data)
- [Harry Potter Characters](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/gulsahdemiryurek/harry-potter-dataset)
- [Spotify Tracks](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/zaheenhamidani/ultimate-spotify-tracks-db)
- [Lego Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/rtatman/lego-database)

## Loading a CSV from Google Drive

If your file is not already at a public URL, put it in a Google Drive folder in your UCSB account
and load it from there:

1. Save the file to a Google Drive folder in your UCSB account.
2. Change the sharing settings to allow anyone with the link to view it.
3. Open the sharing dialog and copy the link.
4. Put this code in the Import Data section at the top of your notebook.

```{python}
#| eval: false
import pandas as pd
import requests

def extract_file_id(url):
    """Extract file id from Google Drive Sharing URL."""
    return url.split("/")[-2]

def df_from_gdrive_csv(url):
    """ Get the CSV file from a Google Drive Sharing URL."""
    file_id = extract_file_id(url)
    URL = "https://docs.google.com/uc?export=download"
    session = requests.Session()
    response = session.get(URL, params={"id": file_id}, stream=True)
    return pd.read_csv(response.raw)

# Example of how to use:
# Note: your sharing link will be different, but should look like this:
sharing_url = "https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RlilHNG7BtvXT2Pm4OpgNvEjVJJZNaps/view?usp=share_link"
df = df_from_gdrive_csv(sharing_url)
df.head()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Check this on Thursday morning, not Friday"}
A Drive link that has not been shared correctly fails silently for everybody except the person who
uploaded it. Have a teammate run the loading cell on their own machine on Day 8, before you build
anything on top of it.
:::
